The most direct reading would be that Burke understands meaning to emerge as our ideas about the world, making meaning the sense or significance of things, events, and relations. We can do more with this insight into the ambience of design than single out and focus on various strands, such as the functional (how usable it is), the cognitive (what it means for us), or the affective (how it makes us feel). Instead, we could build a fresh, cumulative list of things with which we might concern ourselves as teachers, writers, and rhetoricians. If Microsoft perhaps intended more direct forms of marketing and the shaping of the user's experience, including the service of avant-garde musicians to brand Microsoft products, it is important that Eno's music resists such narrowing. For Eno, ambient music is inherently political, evoking new senses of place and how human beings inhabit it; this includes, more pointedly, a reduced role for human agency reflecting a more distributed, ecological approach to will, action, and consequence. The lengthy video session with Robert Fripp and the Microsoft team suggests that such aesthetics and their politics, however indirect, are nevertheless in play. So, while startup music itself makes up only a small element amid these far larger concerns (not to mention the larger expanse of sonic space and its rhetorical-architectural possibilities), possibly one of little relevance, it nevertheless can open us onto a deeper reflection concerning our relation to technology, space, and sonics, and we lose much ifwe ignore the insights it grants.

Thomas Rickert

Philosophy & Rhetoric, Volume 52, Number 1, 2019, pp. 93-101 (Article)

Published by Penn State University Press

It Is All There: From Reason to Reasoning-in-the-World

Thomas Rickert

abstract

The emergence of narratives concerning post-truth, alternative facts, fake news, and the like underpins a felt sense of crisis about the possibility of debate, insofar as argument depends on truth norms. This essay argues that the post-truth narrative is regressive. It depends on Enlightenment-derived standards of truth that were from the beginning impoverished. I argue that rather than appeal nostalgically to the past, we should look to arguments interior to rhetorical history that point to truth norms that include worldly experience, or thereness. Using examples from Protagoras, Johann Georg Hamann, and Maurice Merleau-Ponty, I briefly expand on different ways of conceiving how to marry worldly involvements to our conceptions of knowledge. The world, inclusive of radical technological change, doesn't just shape but takes part in who we are and what we know, say, and do. In this sense, argument and debate are ambient phenomena.

keywords: post-truth, Protagoras, Johann Georg Hamann, ambient, Maurice Merleau-Ponty

Argument and its performance as debate are ambient phenomena. It takes a world to have an argument, and as the world changes, so will the ways and means of argument.The current narratives circulating about post-truth, truthiness, alternative facts, and the like, while illuminating somewhat different registers, gloss this point. Collectively, they seem to assert that truth's sway in public discourse has lessened, threatening the possibility of robust civic discourse and politics. I am leery of such claims. They are in general regressive, since they are nostalgic, working from a rear-view mirror mirage

of stability and surety. Setting aside the panic such writers generate, and considering some deeper implications already within our intellectual histories, we can instead see ourselves on the verge of a real advance in our understandings of truth, argument, and rhetoric. Such an advance calls us to reintegrate reason into the lifeworld and, in so doing, find within the rhetorical tradition what opens new paths forward. Of course, this path is well under way across a variety of fields, such as philosophy, cognitive science, neuroscientific studies of emotion, moral psychology, and more. In various ways this work demonstrates that Enlightenment-derived narratives of truth, rationality, and human being are insufficient. However, here I want to address not this large body of work, but scenes resonant with it that are internal to rhetoric's own development. This, then, is a statement on the possibility of debate not as peak but as plateau.

i was up above it, but now i'm down in it

We can understand these as early theories of radical immanence. There is something amiss when music evokes such paradoxical positions, described simultaneously as powerful, indeterminate, and inessential. Further, beyond the inherent contradictions, these positions seem tainted by various modalities of suspicion that resonate with the ire rhetoric too has continually inspired through the millennia. And if the first argument has its kernel of truth, if, that is, music does affect us deeply, then we must see that music involves rhetoric. It is always somewhere, and this somewhere can never be fully circumscribed by either meaning or symbolicity. We are worldly. Necessarily, our a priori affectability is not just a transaction among animate beings-humans primarily, but as Davis suggests, also nonhuman animals-so that we see this affectability as enmeshed in material locales that give place and bearing prior to symbolicity proper. All being must be part of the giving of what gives, and the world is what is given, both as meaning and as what withdraws from meaning, even ifworld is not equivalently given. Thus, the challenge of this chapter is to think how rhetoric is caught up in the play of language and materiality while raising the specter that neither language nor materiality can be reduced to symbolicity. These questions are themselves problematic from Burke's perspective. Burke almost uniformly places meaning first, and the rhetoricity implicit to symbolic action emerges with it. Such materiality, as I will show in the upcoming chapters, should always be understood across the play of presence and withdrawal, and human being is only one locus for this play.

Many have read Heidegger's remarks on our relations to things as saying that human beings are immersed in the world through language and everyday practices. This perspective suggests, on the one hand, that we cannot break through or extricate ourselves from our emplacement so as to get at things from the "outside," as it were, and, on the other hand, that the things of the world are never trumped by language or ideas. Our holistic entanglements are material and practical first and foremost. Hubert Dreyfus is a well-known proponent of this position and posits Heidegger as a "robust realist," meaning that Heidegger avoids the Scylla ofnaive realism and the Charybdis of idealism ("Coping" n.p.). The world is a participant in the ongoing event of human being-in-the-world, not a stage or backdrop to what human beings do and say. And this is a nuanced participation, with things emerging from and participating in human practices, and human practices in turn requiring things. Such an interpretation is fine as a first take, except that it exhibits a certain skewing: the nexus remains tethered to human being. Human usage and behavior become the privileged means of access to the background, and things, such as tools, light up to our awareness as we use them; then, when our attention shifts elsewhere, they dim back into the shadowy realm of equipment (Zeug) in general, the undifferentiated, always receding backdrop of"stuff."1 Heidegger certainly lends himself to such a reading. Speaking ofa room, he remarks that we encounter it not as a geometrical space but as "equipment for residingp that we have at least discovered, and that discovery and our activities yield

an arrangement that allows individual items to show themselves (BT 98). I take the steps downstairs into the basement, set out my books, organize my papers, boot the laptop, put some Klaus Schulze on the turntable, sit on the chair at the desk, insert the pen drive, enter words into the chapter file (i.e., write), read, take notes, edit, save the file, put on some Dexter Gordon. adjust the stereo volume, and so forth, with aspects of the room now near and now far from my attentions and activities. In various ways, these things all go together; there is an arrangement from which individual entities already derive their place wherefrom I can weave them through my activities. Entities in turn show up and dim back into the recesses as my attention flows variously through my purposeful activity.

In Tool-Being Graham Harman argues that such readings, reminiscent of Dreyfus, are not wrong but nevertheless miss something crucial to the nature of equipment and objects. Objects can no more be positioned solely within the horizon of human intention or awareness than language can. My example of the basement illustrates this tendency, since everything has its "nearness" and "farness" in relation to my attentions and intentions. One could of course add more history here and pile on thick description across the attentions and intentions of other people, social roles, and equipment. But none of this suffices to give us any ultimate grip on the object. Harman argues that "ifwe could total up all the 'contexts, roles, and social goals' in which a specific bridge or flagpole are currently embedded, this would still not give us the being of these objects" (TB 124). Any use or meaning that I or anyone else can bring, or even the plenitude of people, uses, contexts, histories, and other objects that could be brought forward, only serves to present some particular qualities out of the object's fulsomeness, or what Harman calls its "grand, dark abundance" (TB 125). Indeed. as the new wave of cognitive science (such as the work of Andy Clark, Paul Dourish, Anthony Chemero, and so on) demonstrates, the use of tools and local environmental scaffolding inspires changes in our sense of embodiment, blurring boundaries; to use a computer mouse, for instance, amounts to making that mouse part of one's body, and in so doing, it effectively disappears.8 Thus, predicating ontological distinctions on human attention and its shifting cognitive and bodily boundaries is fruitless; the ontological has to manifest beyond such human-derived loci, and thus withdrawal does not depend on human perception or any other singular interaction.

Ambient music, I am arguing, brings together at a practical level many of the thematic strands I have been discussing, including ambience's connection to rhetoricity. 20 It evokes the concreteness of place through various experiential registers, both for audience and composer, richly enough to constitute what I mean by situation (thought here in terms of Befindlichkeit), the affective, material disposition in which one finds oneself. Thus, the local environs are not background for music's emergence but, in countless ways, an active player in their own right: from the sourcing of found sound (sea bells, insects, or wind and rain); to the acoustic properties of the recording environment, whether "natural" (the previously mentioned Headley Grange for Led Zeppelin) or "artificial" (the drained, empty, electronically produced echo of Joy Division as engineered by the producer Martin Hannett on Unknown Pleasures); to the use of equipment in the composing process itself (turntables for DJs, amplifiers to produce feedback, or tape loops) (see Fuller 13-53); or even to the creation of "impossible'' places realized through the artifice of sound (Eno'sAmbient 4: On Land and Eno and Hass ell's Fourth World, Vol. 1: Possible Musics). The latter point connects back to Clark's assertion about "the ways that the body and the local environment are literally built into the processing loops that result in intelligent action" (Being xii), except here, it is not always action but sometimes experience.

Let me strengthen the connection here between rhetoric, music, and place. The world reveals itself in a musical way, but it does so in such fashion as to transform our experience of place itself. Ambient rhetoric, analogically, brings the world to us but in doing so transforms the disposition of our inhabitancy. This, as I have stated already, is my reworking of what rhetoric is: the world is revealed differently, at least potentially so, in a way that calls for some action. By implication, rhetoric from an ambient perspective can no longer be situated solely in human subjective performance.

Ambient music sounds out the importance of place in conceiving not just rhetoric's performative work but also rhetoricity itself as worldly affectabilityprior to symbolicity.

Indeed, the importance that ambient music attributes to place has wider implications about the power of place as a general and significant matter in its own right. Issues of space and place have gathered momentum in the twentieth century, in the work of Gaston Bachelard, Henri Lefebvre, Alfred North Whitehead, Michel Foucault. Edward Soja, and many more. Heidegger has also been important here, as is borne out especially in the work of Edward Casey, who has done much to put place back into theoretical dis-

cussion (see The Fate of Place). As I discuss in chapter 1, on the chiira, place has since Aristotle largely been conceived categorically and transcendentally, so that place is assimilated to space (Casey x). Heidegger gives back to place its thick particularity; instead of being just another locatable site within a generalized spatial matrix, place becomes habitation. a material. unique location wherein people and things are situated (Casey 20; see also Walter). As Heidegger says, the ambient environs, the '"round-about[.]' is not at all defined by a being-located-side-by-side-and-around-each-other and by geometrical relations, but rather it is the round-about of worldly dealings with it which are concerned about it, attend to it, and go around in it" (0 79). Meaning, affect. and attachment become integral to place, and as ambient music also shows us, "place is indeed an active source ofpresencing: within its close embrace, things get located and begin to happen" (Casey 63). And here we can return full circle to my first, ancient example, the caves at Lascaux. Lascaux is a source of presencing involving the full range of early human existence, including its specific comportment toward aspects of the nonhuman. It is not just a location that happens to be the bearer of early aesthetic and ritualistic designs but a unique place that was integral to their emergence, a kind of window on how the world worlded for them (despite the fact that we may not know the actual details and import of this work). Our traditional sense of aesthetics, among other things, tends to sunder the "art" from the mundane materiality of the cave itself, but this occludes how the material environment is itself already part of what the "art" is. In discussing persuasion, we risk the same reductive move when we exclude the full range of ambient, material phenomena. When we want to examine, say, Howard Dean's 2004 Democratic nomination race "I have a scream" speech, we cannot divorce such discussion from the material environments in which the "scream" emerged, environments that were integral to how it was understood, from the auditorium for the live audience
